Supporting basis
std::sort is the superior choice due to its highly optimized Introsort algorithm, which combines QuickSort, HeapSort, and InsertionSort. While custom QuickSort relies on average-case performance, std::sort guarantees O(n log n) worst-case complexity by switching to HeapSort upon detecting deep recursion, effectively preventing catastrophic O(n^2) behavior on adversarial inputs. Although uniform distributions are generally favorable for QuickSort, standard library implementations leverage decades of compiler and hardware-specific optimizations, such as efficient branch prediction and cache-aware memory access patterns. Furthermore, std::sort handles pivot selection intelligently, often using median-of-three or similar strategies that minimize partitioning overhead. For 10 million doubles, the marginal gain from a custom implementation is negligible compared to the robustness and lower latency provided by the standard library, which is rigorously tuned for diverse hardware architectures.

Recommendation
Use std::sort without hesitation. Its consistent performance and guaranteed worst-case complexity make it significantly more reliable than a naive custom QuickSort, which risks severe slowdowns on specific data patterns despite the uniform distribution. The standard library’s implementation is heavily optimized for modern CPUs, utilizing instruction-level parallelism and efficient memory management that would require extensive effort to replicate manually. For practical production systems, readability and maintainability also favor std::sort, reducing bug potential and technical debt. Empirical benchmarks consistently show std::sort matching or exceeding hand-written sorts in real-world scenarios due to these low-level optimizations. Therefore, relying on std::sort ensures maximum performance, safety, and code clarity, making it the optimal solution for sorting 10,000,000 uniform double-precision values efficiently and robustly in any professional C++ application.<|im_end|>
